Designing Channel Creation from a One-Line Requirement

Turning "we need channel creation" into a validated, 150-field, multi-section stepper system, built shoulder-to-shoulder with Solution Architecture and Engineering, and evolved across a dozen releases without ever breaking its own design language.

02 Executive Summary

One line of requirement. 150 fields of real complexity.

Channel Creation began as a single sentence: "we need to build channel creation." There was no spec, no field list, no wireframe to inherit, just a business need. What followed was months of close, three-way collaboration between UX, Solution Architecture and Engineering to discover, name and structure every field the platform actually needed to launch a channel.

As Solution Developer, Solution Architect and Senior Developer surfaced fields (and, along the way, entire sub-features like Bouquet Management and Catalogue linking), I owned turning that steadily growing list into something a human being could fill in without giving up. That meant deciding, field by field, which section it belonged to, building a validated multi-step stepper, and adding a Preview step so nobody submits a channel they haven't actually reviewed.

My Role

UX Designer, UX Architect, UI Designer and Solution Design partner, from field taxonomy through final pixel and dev handoff.

Collaborators

Solution Developer, Solution Architect and Senior Developer, co-defining fields, logic and constraints together.

Scale

~150 recognised fields, grouped into General, Delivery, Security, Enablers and Advertisement sections.

Lifespan

Re-designed across a dozen+ iterations as new requirements landed, without breaking the core pattern.

The short version

The Starting Point

A single-line requirement with no field list. Every piece of scope had to be discovered collaboratively before it could be designed.

The Approach

Group 150 fields by real meaning, split them across a validated stepper, and force a Preview before anything goes live.

The Outcome

A reusable Create/Update pattern that later absorbed Recording, safe Deletion, and full Ingestion tracking without a redesign.

04 Discovery & Field Taxonomy

Recognising 150 fields, one working session at a time.

This wasn't a solo UX exercise. It was co-designed. Solution Developer, Solution Architect and Senior Developer sat with me session after session, surfacing every field the platform needed to launch and operate a channel.

Feature areas discovered along the way

Channel Creation didn't stay a single form for long. As fields were grouped, entire feature areas revealed themselves inside what had looked like one flat requirement.

Bouquet Management Catalogue Linking Delivery Configuration Security & DRM Enablers Advertisement
The core UX problem

~150 fields cannot live in one form. Long forms fail for well-known reasons: users lose their place, validation errors compound, and abandonment climbs the moment scrolling replaces scanning. This needed structure, not just a bigger page.

05 Information Architecture

Every field earned its section. Nothing was grouped by guesswork.

As UX Architect, I mapped each of the ~150 fields to the section it conceptually belonged to, then ordered those sections into a stepper so operators move through the channel logically: what it is, how it's delivered, how it's protected, what turns it on, how it's monetised.

Channel Creation Stepper · Section Ownership
  • Channel Type Selection entry step
  • General ~30 fields
    • Basic metadata, names & descriptions per language, dates, definition, category
  • Delivery ~35 fields
    • Broadcast & OTT delivery configuration, origin, streaming parameters
  • Security ~30 fields
    • DRM, watermarking, entitlement and access-control rules
  • Enablers ~20 fields
    • Feature flags that switch channel-level capabilities on or off
  • Advertisement ~20 fields
    • Ad insertion, monetisation and campaign-linked configuration
  • Preview review step

Field counts are approximate groupings from the working sessions. The real number in production is close to 150 across all sections.

06 Key UX Decisions

Five decisions that made 150 fields feel manageable.

1 · Stepper over single form

Every field lives in exactly one section; operators complete one focused step at a time instead of scrolling an endless page.

2 · Validation gates the Next button

The Next action stays disabled until every mandatory field in the current step is filled. Invalid states are prevented, not corrected after the fact.

3 · Preview before submit

Because a channel is business-critical, the final step is always a full read-only review of everything entered before any create action fires.

4 · Confirmation before create

Submitting from Preview asks for one more explicit confirmation, so a channel is never created by accident.

5 · One pattern, every lifecycle stage

The same stepper + preview pattern was reused for Update, so operators never have to learn a second mental model.

07 Final Solution · Channel Record

150 fields, captured. But never all on screen at once.

Once a channel is created, its record reuses the same sectioned structure as the stepper: General Details expanded by default, with Delivery, Security, Advertisement and Videos collapsed until an operator actually needs them.

08 Final Solution · Channel Listing

One table, every distribution type.

Channels split across Commercial TV, Commercial Radio, FAST O&O, FAST 3PP and App Launch Point, so the listing uses tabs to keep each distribution type legible, with inline General / Broadcast / OTT groupings so operators can scan enablement state at a glance.

1
Add Channel, always in reachThe most common action sits top-right, consistent with every other entity list in the console.
2
Distribution-type tabsCommercial TV, Commercial Radio, FAST O&O, FAST 3PP and App Launch Point each get their own scoped table instead of one overloaded list.
3
Inline Enable / WM / DRM togglesBroadcast and OTT states are editable directly from the row. No need to open the full record for a quick toggle.
4
Edit, view, delete, save (inline)Every row carries its own action set, keeping bulk operational work inside the listing itself.
09 Final Solution · Save Safety

Inline edits on a 400-channel table are exactly where mistakes happen.

Because the listing allows direct inline edits, two guardrails were non-negotiable: never let an operator lose unsaved work by navigating away, and never let a save happen without one explicit confirmation naming the exact channel affected.

1

Leave without saving? Triggers the instant an operator tries to navigate away with unsaved inline edits, giving them a clear Leave / Stay choice.

2

Confirm before save Names the specific Channel ID being changed, so a confirmation click is never ambiguous about what it affects.

10 Final Solution · Operation Tracking

Creating a channel isn't instant, so the UI says so.

Channel create, update and delete all trigger backend ingestion jobs that take real time to complete. Rather than leaving operators guessing, every operation gets a tracked status: Processing, Completed, or Failed, each stage named, not just a spinner.

1
2
3
4
1
Immediate confirmation toastThe moment a create/update/delete is submitted, a toast confirms the job has been accepted before the page even reloads.
2
Completed, with a timestampA finished job shows both start and end time, useful for support teams reconciling "when did this actually go live."
3
Named processing stagesProcessing shows the exact stage (Merging, Transforming, Matching or Publishing), so operators see exactly which stage a job is in, not just a generic loading state.
4
Failed, with a way inA failed job surfaces immediately in the same list, with a direct "View Details" link into the failure reason.
11 Final Solution · Failure Detail

"It failed" is never good enough for an enterprise operator.

Clicking into a failed job opens a detail panel with exactly what a support engineer needs to act: the channel and job identifiers, the time window, an error code, and a human-readable failure reason pulled straight from the backend service that failed.

1
2
3
4
1
Dedicated failure panelOpens in-place from the ingestion list, no separate module to hunt through. Echoes the same "stay in context" principle from the audit-history redesign.
2
Channel ID & Name togetherBoth identifiers shown side by side so support can cross-reference the exact record without leaving the panel.
3
Explicit error codeA real HTTP-style error code (e.g. 403) gives engineering a concrete starting point instead of a vague "something went wrong."
4
Human-readable failure reasonThe exact backend message (service name, channel ID and job ID) surfaced verbatim, so no one has to dig through logs to reproduce it.
12 The Update Flow

Updating reuses everything, except Preview now has one extra job.

Channel Update runs through the exact same sectioned stepper as Creation, so operators never learn a second interaction model. The one deliberate difference lives in Preview: instead of just showing final values, it highlights precisely which fields changed from the previous saved version, a smaller, faster cousin of the Version Comparison pattern from the audit-history redesign.

Illustrative recreation · Update Preview, changed-field highlight
Channel NameStar Plus

Channel DefinitionUltra High Definition
Channel Audio Language+ Tamil added

Recreated here for clarity. The production Preview uses the same amber "Updated" semantic already established for version comparison elsewhere in the console, so the visual language never has to be relearned.

13 Deletion Safety Constraint

A channel with millions of viewers cannot be deleted casually.

If a channel stayed enabled while being deleted, a recording could be initiated by any one of millions of active viewers in that exact window, creating orphaned recordings tied to a channel that no longer exists. So deletion was designed as a sequence, not a single action.

01Attempt to delete an enabled channel
→
✕Blocked: channel must be disabled first
→
02Disable the channel
↓
05Channel deletion now allowed
←
04All recordings deleted
←
03Recordings still exist? Must delete them first
Why disable first

Disabling stops new recordings from being initiated by any of the channel's active viewers before deletion proceeds.

Why recordings must go first

Deleting a channel while recordings still reference it would orphan that data, so recordings are a hard prerequisite, not a warning.

14 The Recording Feature

A feature added long after launch, without touching the core pattern.

Recording shipped after Channel Creation had already been live for a while. Operators can open a channel's recordings directly from its detail page via a dedicated CTA, and view recordings scoped either by account or by channel, with every recording linked back to the specific account that initiated it.

Entry point

A "Recordings" action sits directly on the Channel Details page (see it annotated in Section 07).

Two scopes

Recordings can be viewed by Account ID or by Channel ID, matching how support teams actually investigate issues.

Traceable ownership

Every recording is linked to the specific account that triggered it, never an anonymous, unattributed entry.

15 Design Evolution

This never shipped once. It shipped a dozen times.

New requirements kept arriving well after the first release: new fields, new sections, new validation rules. Every iteration was aligned back to the same sectioned stepper and Preview pattern instead of forking into a one-off redesign. 16 Impact

From an unscoped ask to a system that kept absorbing new scope.

No production analytics existed for this internal console, so these numbers are directional: field counts and iteration history tracked from Figma version logs and release notes, confirmed with Product and Engineering rather than pulled from usage data.

Error Prevention ↑

Validation gates Next; nothing invalid can move forward.

Review Confidence ↑

17 Lessons Learned

What a one-line requirement taught me.

Discovery is a design activity

Sitting with Solution Architecture and Engineering to name 150 fields was UX work. The form couldn't be designed until the scope was.

Structure beats scale

150 fields aren't a UX problem once they're correctly grouped. The section, not the field count, is what determines usability.

One pattern, many lifecycle stages

Designing Create, Update, Delete and Recording as one evolving pattern, instead of four separate features, is what let the system absorb new requirements safely.

Safety constraints deserve their own flow

The disable-before-delete sequence wasn't an edge case to patch on. It was designed as a first-class part of the deletion flow.

18 Final Reflection
"A one-line requirement isn't a shortcut. It's an invitation to design the scope itself, not just the screen.

Channel Creation started with almost nothing written down and grew into one of the most structurally important systems in the console, not because the form got more complex, but because the taxonomy underneath it was designed to keep absorbing complexity without breaking.
